opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started as a tool rather than a goal. When we were working on the lottery ticket hypothesis, we had this puzzle: on small networks you could rewind to initialization, prune, and retrain to full accuracy, but on bigger networks like ResNets on ImageNet, that just didn't work. We needed a way to ask, "What's different about the cases where it works and the cases where it doesn't?" And accuracy alone wasn't telling us much.

So the question we asked was about stability. Take a network at some point in training, make two copies, and train each one with different SGD noise, meaning different data orders and different augmentation. Then linearly interpolate between the two final networks and see whether the loss goes up along that path. If it doesn't, if there's no barrier, then in a meaningful sense those two runs ended up in the same basin. The outcome of optimization was determined by that starting point, not by the noise.

What made it compelling to me is that it's a very cheap, very concrete test of a very abstract idea. People talk about loss landscapes in vague terms, with pictures of hills and valleys that don't really reflect millions of dimensions. Linear interpolation is something you can actually measure, and the answer is surprisingly crisp. Early in training, networks are unstable: two copies end up separated by a big barrier. Then, fairly early, often within the first few percent of training, they become stable, and from that point on the copies are linearly connected. And that transition lined up remarkably well with when lottery ticket rewinding started to work. That's the kind of correlation that tells you you're measuring something real about the dynamics.

I'd also be careful not to overclaim. Being linearly connected doesn't mean the networks are identical, and a barrier doesn't mean they're fundamentally different. Permutation symmetries complicate things a lot. But as a lens on when the important decisions in training get made, I find it one of the more useful measurements we have. It suggests that a lot of training is a chaotic early phase followed by something much more like settling into a valley, and that's a really interesting thing to understand if you care about why deep learning works at all.

r001.rationale: The response presents barrier-free linear connectivity as a measurable indicator of training stability and says its transition aligns with when lottery-ticket rewinding works, distinguishing runs with different properties.

r002.rationale: The response describes interpolating between networks and checking for a loss barrier, but does not say this indicates whether averaging them produces a useful network.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that I didn't start out caring about the loss landscape at all. I was trying to understand why lottery tickets work, and more specifically why they stop working. If you take a big network, train it, prune it, and rewind the surviving weights to initialization, that sparse subnetwork trains just fine on something like MNIST. On ImageNet, or ResNet-50, it falls apart. You have to rewind not to step zero but to some early point in training, maybe a few percent of the way in, and then it works again. And I had no explanation for that. It was just an empirical fact I kept bumping into.

The way we eventually made sense of it was through what we called instability to SGD noise. Take a network at some point in training, make two copies, and train each one with a different random data order. Then ask a very simple question: if I draw a straight line between the two trained networks in weight space and evaluate the loss along it, does it go up? If there's a big barrier in the middle, the two runs ended up in genuinely different places. If it's flat, they ended up in what's effectively the same basin, and the noise of SGD didn't actually matter for where you landed.

What made that interesting to me is that it lined up almost exactly with the lottery ticket results. The point in training where the full network becomes stable, where those two copies start landing in the same linearly connected region, is the same point where you can rewind a sparse subnetwork to and have it train to full accuracy. Rewinding earlier than that, the subnetwork is still unstable, it gets knocked into a worse basin, and you lose accuracy. So it stopped being a curiosity and became an explanation.

I'll be careful about what I claim the metric means in some deep sense. Linear mode connectivity is a very crude probe. It's one line through a very high-dimensional space, and the fact that there's no barrier along that line doesn't tell you the basin is convex in any rigorous way. What I'd say it tells you is that the two solutions are interchangeable from the optimizer's point of view. And that's the thing I actually care about, because so much of what we do in practice, pruning, fine-tuning, deciding when a run has "committed," depends on whether the early part of training has already locked in the outcome. This gives you a way to measure that, with a plain experiment anyone can run, rather than arguing about it from intuition.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing whether two training runs lie in the same linearly connected region and links that result to whether a rewound sparse network can reach full accuracy, making it an empirical discriminator of outcomes.

r002.rationale: The response discusses loss barriers, shared regions, and optimizer interchangeability, but does not explain whether averaging the networks can produce a useful network.

astra-6.text:
To me, it’s a way of making the question “Did these networks learn the same thing?” a little more concrete. Two networks can have the same accuracy, but that doesn’t tell you whether training found essentially the same solution or two very different solutions.

So you can take the weights of one network and interpolate in a straight line to the weights of the other. If the loss stays low along that path, that suggests they’re part of the same connected low-loss region. If there’s a big loss barrier in between, then there’s some meaningful difference between where they ended up.

I’d be careful about calling that proof that they’re in the same convex region—you’ve only checked a line, and neural networks have symmetries that complicate the picture. But it’s a useful operational test. It lets us ask whether changing something about training changes the solution we find, rather than just whether it changes the final accuracy.

r001.rationale: The response presents low loss along a straight-line interpolation as a useful test for whether networks share a connected low-loss region, but explicitly says this does not prove they occupy the same convex region.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss averaging the networks or whether averaging them would produce a useful network.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, two networks can have the same accuracy and still be doing very different things. So if you want to ask whether two training runs found essentially the same solution, you need something richer than just comparing their test accuracies.

One fairly concrete thing you can do is interpolate between their weights and measure the loss along that line. If the loss stays low, that suggests the two solutions are in the same basin, at least in this operational sense. If the loss shoots up in between, then there’s a barrier separating them.

I wouldn’t say that proves they’re computing the same function, or that checking one line establishes a whole convex region. But it gives us a useful, testable notion of similarity. You can then ask: how much does changing the random seed, the order of the data, or some early part of training actually change where the network ends up? That’s a much more interesting question to me than whether the final accuracies happen to match.

r001.rationale: The response presents low-loss interpolation as evidence that two trained networks share a basin and calls it a useful, testable measure of similarity, even while cautioning that one line does not establish an entire convex region.

r002.rationale: The response discusses interpolation as a similarity measure but does not explain whether averaging the networks can produce a useful network.
